paras: The Export Lumber Company strike assault was an attack in Brooklyn, New York, in about September 1903, in which white lumber handlers on strike threatened Black lumbermen hired to replace them and four of the strikers beat one of the Black workers. The four were arrested, and a magistrate fined one of them $2 and discharged the others after they said they objected to their jobs going to Black men. The case is known only from an Atlanta Constitution editorial that used it to taunt the Brooklyn minister Newell Dwight Hillis over Northern race prejudice.

According to the editorial, which drew on New York papers, the white handlers of the Export Lumber Company struck "a few weeks" earlier for time-and-a-half pay for overtime work. To fill their places, the company sent South and hired a "gang of negro lumbermen."

Once the Black lumbermen began work, the strikers harassed them and, in the editorial's words, threatened them "with deaths of divers and sundry kinds." Four strikers then attacked one of the Black workers and beat him; the editorial did not name him or describe his injuries.

The four strikers were arrested and pleaded that they objected to having their jobs given to Black men rather than white men. The magistrate accepted the plea, fining the leader $2 and discharging the other three. The coverage names none of the strikers, the victim or the magistrate.

The episode reached print in the surviving coverage only as Southern commentary: the Atlanta Constitution's editorial "A Case For Dr. Hillis" was reprinted by the Gold Leaf of Henderson, North Carolina, on October 15, 1903. The editorial called the dispute a "race war" and recounted the beating in mocking terms, describing the victim as a "poor colored brother" beaten "like he was a bass drum" and his attackers as "nigger-punchers." Its purpose was to turn Hillis's criticism of Southern "race prejudice" back on Brooklyn, suggesting he go to the lumber yards and "stand substitute" for the Black workers.
No original New York report of the strike or the court case, and no Black-press coverage, was found.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution editorial (from New York papers)
accounts.gist: White lumber handlers struck, the company hired Black lumbermen from the South, strikers threatened them, four beat one, and a magistrate fined one $2 and discharged three after they said they objected to Black men taking their jobs.

framing.detail: Headed 'A Case For Dr. Hillis', the editorial treated the beating as a joke at a Northern critic's expense, calling the attackers 'nigger-punchers' and the victim a 'poor colored brother' beaten 'like he was a bass drum', while pointing to Northern race prejudice.
